criteria.semantics: Claimed natively: a native <meter> with a <label for> matching its unique id; value, min, max, low, high and optimum as numeric attributes (defaults 0, 1, min, max, midpoint). Visible text beside it states the value, bounds, thresholds, optimum and assessment, so a reading beyond the range stays explicit though the bar clamps.

keyboard.outcome: Passes it by: it is not a stop in the tab order.

criteria.name: The meter's label, the same words as the visible label.
criteria.role: Meter, with its value in its range.
criteria.group: The reading in words, after the meter.

setting.statement: WHEN I set my text size to 200% I SEE the label and the reading grow with it, with no loss of information.
WHEN I zoom the page to 400% I SEE the label, the bar and the reading wrap in place, with no horizontal scrolling.

check.statement: The face emits a native <meter> element.
I SEE a label that stays visible, tied to the meter by for and id, with the meter's label as its text.
The meter's value, min and max are the model's.
A meter is not a control: nothing in it is a stop in the tab order.
WHEN I reach the meter with a desktop screen reader (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver) I HEAR its label, the role of meter and its value.
WHEN I read on I HEAR the reading in words: the value, its bounds and its assessment.

criteria.semantics: Claimed natively: a noninteractive palette bar (accent on surface, warn for a suboptimal region, danger for the region farthest from optimum or a value beyond the bounds), with the same reading in words beside it as on html: color only reinforces words. It adds no tab stop. Once GPUI exposes a tree: an AccessKit Meter with its value and range (AXLevelIndicator on macOS, a ProgressBar with the RangeValue pattern on Windows, a level bar on AT-SPI).

keyboard.outcome: Pass the meter by: it is no stop of its own; the controls before and after it are.

criteria.name: The meter's label.

setting.statement: WHEN I set the system text size to 200% (Windows' Accessibility, Text size; GNOME's Large Text or text scaling factor) I SEE the label and the reading grow with it, with no loss of information.

WHEN I raise the display scale (macOS' Displays, Larger Text; Windows' Scale at 150% or 200%; GNOME's Scale at 200%) I SEE the label and the reading drawn sharp and larger, whole and without overlapping.

WHEN I turn on the platform's high contrast (macOS' Increase contrast, a Windows contrast theme, the desktop portal's contrast) I SEE the window switch to the high-contrast palette by itself, the label and the reading at 7:1.
WHEN I choose the high-contrast theme for the window I SEE the label and the reading drawn in the high-contrast palette, every pair at 7:1.
WHEN I magnify the screen (macOS Zoom, Windows Magnifier, GNOME's Zoom) I SEE the label and the reading whole and legible in the magnified view.

check.statement: A meter adds no stop to the window's tab order.
I SEE the reading and its assessment in words beside the bar, not only in its color.
WHEN I reach the meter with VoiceOver (macOS), Narrator (Windows) or Orca (Linux) I HEAR its label, its value in its range, and the reading in words.

announce.api: AXLevelIndicator with AXValue, AXMinValue and AXMaxValue (AccessKit Role::Meter).
ControlType ProgressBar with the RangeValue pattern (Value, Minimum, Maximum), read-only.

criteria.note: GPUI 0.2.2 exposes no accessibility tree (no AccessKit, NSAccessibility, UI Automation or AT-SPI provider), so every HEAR check is blocked by the toolkit, and so are the system text size and the platform's high contrast, which it does not report. GPUI's main branch has AccessKit (zed-industries/zed#56065), not yet released (gpui/README.md, "Accessibility tree"). Its SEE checks with a probe run on GPUI's test platform (gpui/src/native.rs, every_gpui_see_check_with_a_probe_holds), which no CI job runs yet; the rest are reported as not verified.
